newsitem.title: UK: Shirt-sleeved Major shows new skill as comic.
newsitem.headline: Shirt-sleeved Major shows new skill as comic.

text.p: Why did Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi use a big plane to fly to the European summit in Dublin last weekend?
Because he had his country's budget deficit with him.
The quip is part of the routine of the latest stand-up comedian to thrill punters at a British seaside resort.
His managers believe they have a winner.
His identity? Prime Minister John Major.

With the odds against a fifth successive election victory for his Conservative Party rising by the day, the grey man has become the funny man. Even if there is no proof the tactic is a vote-winner, his audiences seem to like it.

Ditching the formal speech-making of the Conservatives' annual conference, a shirt-sleeved Major regaled ruling party supporters on Tuesday with anecdotes about his meetings with world leaders like Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
Prowling the stage with a radio microphone attached to his belt, Major made fun of himself as a man with little fashion sense and a liking for homely sweaters.

Revealing the intimate moments of a world leader, he chatted about his walk two years ago near Chequers, the British premier's country home, alone with Yeltsin -- alone, that is, except for security officers, policemen and press photographers.
With perfect comic timing Major told how, as they walked and discussed weighty world affairs, a neighbour of Chequers out walking her dogs came face to face with the two leaders.
Without missing a stride, the woman marched on, saying "Morning, Prime Minister. Morning, Mr President." An astounded Yeltsin told Major: "Now I know why you won the war."
Just to underline, the conference performance was not an aberration, Major also turns up as a diarist in this weekend's edition of the right-wing poltitical weekly, The Spectator.
At least one person was amused by his joke about the Italian prime minister, Major writes. Prodi himself.
In a chatty column detailing the lighter side of power, Major said Prodi agreed with the quip about the deficit.
"He had high hopes, he said, of leaving it behind when he returned to Italy," Major wrote.

Between making fun of photographers, celebrities invited to a reception at the prime minister's Downing Street office and of ministers preparing their conference speeches, Major revealed the true reason he left the European summit early.
Dismissing media reports he was snubbing other European leaders, Major said he could exclusively reveal that it was the weekend of the 26th anniversary of his wedding to Norma.
"Given a choice between dinner with Norma or 15 men, Norma won hands down," Major quipped.

The media have been delighted by the new image for a politician dismissed by critics as dull and uninspiring, and once damningly described by an unnamed colleage as "a man who brings a welcome touch of grey to any colourful occasion".
But behind the quips and jokes is a deadly serious intent. Trailing by 20 points or more in the polls, Major is fighting for his political survival with an election due by May.

Party strategists credit a tour of the country just before the last election, when Major literally climbed on a soapbox to talk to crowds, as the key factor that gave the Conservatives a fourth term in office despite polls predicting defeat.

Strategists believe that contrasting Major's homespun philosophy and down-to-earth image with the slick presentation of his rival, Labour leader Tony Blair, could just be enough to win over voters disenchanted with politicians in general.
Now back to the show. What happened when he and Yeltsin arrived at a pub, only to find it closed?
An aide knocked and asked the landlord to open up, saying: "It's the president of Russia." Back came the reply from inside: "And I'm the Kaiser." Major had them rolling in the aisles.
